node.label: Laurentian & national tradition
node.period_rationale: period_0, 'Earlier roots & interwar initiatives': the tradition's founding works are interwar (Mackintosh 1923, Innis 1930, Creighton 1937), and its cited core in 2009–2026 PhDs runs from Innis 1930 to Berger 1986 (median 1969). Postwar consolidation (Lower 1946, Careless 1954, the Centenary Series from 1964) follows within the main period. Chosen as for Annales and the US Progressives; not an end date.
node.date_label: Staple studies 1923–40 · Creighton 1937 · Lower 1946 · Careless 1954 · Centenary Series volumes 1964–85 · Berger's analysis 1976 · coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1923 is an early economic interpretation, not the tradition's origin; the tradition has no end date, and its works remain in use (Fur Trade cited by 49 PhDs, 2009–2026).

node.description: English-Canadian historical writing that took the transcontinental nation-state as its frame, from the interwar years to the centennial. Its economic core is the staple approach: Innis's studies of the fur trade (1930) and cod fisheries (1940) read Canada's development through exports to imperial centres, an approach Watkins later called Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy. Creighton's Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) simplified and expanded Innis's thesis, making Montreal's merchants the 'spiritual fathers' of Confederation; his Macdonald biography followed. Liberal nationalists such as Lower and Underhill and conservative nationalists such as Creighton and Stacey disagreed politically while sharing the nation-state as the frame of reference. Careless offered a metropolitan interpretation (1954), which urban historians later found indeterminate, and Morton asked in 1946 on what critical premises the established interpretations rested. The Canadian Centenary Series, from 1964, gathered national syntheses, including translated volumes by the Quebec historians Trudel and Ouellet. Cook's and Careless's 'limited identities' (1967, 1969) and the new regional history of Acadiensis (1971) challenged the frame, and Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analysed the English-Canadian tradition as a historiographical subject. French-Canadian historians such as Michel Brunet pursued a rival national vision, treated under Quebec historiography.
node.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not one school. The staple approach (political economy), Creighton's Laurentian narrative, liberal and conservative nationalisms, metropolitanism and the Centenary Series are distinct projects; roster inclusion is not membership. The label avoids 'Laurentian school': no checked source uses that phrase. French-Canadian and Quebec national historiography belongs to quebec_historiography: Trudel and Ouellet are named only in the Centenary Series strand, and the Creighton–Brunet comparison is carried by the relationship note, not the roster. Stacey (official history, external policy) is placed in cdn_military and cdn_political_national; Stanley appears as a secondary row for The Birth of Western Canada. Critics appear as critics.

node.label: English-Canadian intellectual & cultural history
node.period_rationale: Berger (1970, 1976), McKillop (1979) and Owram (1980, 1986) fall in "Reorientations, c. 1970–85"; the cultural-history turn (McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999) is period_3.
node.date_label: Berger 1970, 1976 · McKillop 1979 · Owram 1980, 1986 · cultural turn: McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999 · coverage through 2000; post-2000 extension partial

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. Earlier histories of Canadian ideas belong partly to the national tradition; 1970 is the first selected work and 2016 the latest. Neither bounds the field.

node.description: English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history studies how Canadians thought about empire, nation, religion, science and the state, and later how traditions, myths and public memories were made. Carl Berger's The Sense of Power (1970) examined imperialist ideas of Canadian character and mission and argued that Canadian imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism; his The Writing of Canadian History (1976) made English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject. A. B. McKillop, Marlene Shore and Doug Owram followed ideas into the university, social science, western expansion and the interwar 'service state'. Ramsay Cook's The Regenerators (1985) joined the field to religious history. Critics charged it with what Clarence Karr (1989) called a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology': group biographies of academics, journalists and clergy that said little about what most Canadians thought. Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979) had argued that a field anchored to nationalism left women almost invisible. From the 1990s a cultural history of invention and memory took over much of the ground. Ian McKay's The Quest of the Folk (1994) showed tourism promoters and cultural producers refashioning Nova Scotians as a simple folk. Daniel Francis wrote on the 'imaginary Indian' and national myths, and Jonathan Vance on the memory of the First World War. H. V. Nelles, Keith Walden, E. A. Heaman and Ian Radforth studied pageants, exhibitions and royal tours, and Colin Coates and Cecilia Morgan the commemoration of heroines. Yvan Lamonde's social history of ideas in Quebec runs on a separate francophone track.
node.scope_note: English-Canadian by design; Quebec's histoire sociale des idées is a comparison (Lamonde). Intellectual history (ideas, intellectuals, the university) and cultural history (spectacle, myth, memory) are distinct strands with different methods. The religious strand is shared with cdn_religion_reform, postwar identity with cdn_sixties. Editorial observation, not a sourced claim: Indigenous people appear in this field mostly as settler representations (Francis, Heaman), which is a limit to flag in teaching. PhD evidence (2009–2026): engagement with the field's anchor scholars is steady (ratio 1.02; 1.14 in a fixed panel of 14 universities), while its older works are cited less; the classics are ageing, not the field. Owram's 'Intellectual History in the Land of Limited Identities' (JCS 24:3, 1989; abstract checked, not cited as a source) is a practitioner's self-assessment that also notes the field's nationalist roots and the differing methods of francophone and anglophone writers; it is not treated as a critique.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Berger, The Sense of Power (1970), The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 1986), Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983); Cook, The Maple Leaf Forever (1971), The Regenerators (1985); McKillop, A Disciplined Intelligence (1979), Matters of Mind (1994); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980), The Government Generation (1986); Shore, The Science of Social Redemption (1987); Litt (1992); Vipond (1992); Francis, The Imaginary Indian (1992), National Dreams (1997); McKay, The Quest of the Folk (1994); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Walden (1997); Heaman, The Inglorious Arts of Peace (1999); Nelles, The Art of Nation-Building (1999); Coates and Morgan, Heroines and History (2002); Radforth, Royal Spectacle (2004); Igartua (2006). Critiques: Trofimenkoff, “Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History” (1979); Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” (1989). Comparisons: Lamonde, Histoire sociale des idées au Québec (2000); Lears, No Place of Grace (1981).

representative_people.name: Carl Berger
representative_people.context: Studies the ideas of Canadian imperialists (character, mission, loyalism, militarism), which he argued were one form of Canadian nationalism, and makes English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject.

node.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada

node.description: Historical writing on Christianity as a force in Canadian reform, culture and everyday life, and on whether and when Canada secularized. Its central argument came in 1985–96. Ramsay Cook’s The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social criticism as the sacred becoming secular, and David Marshall’s Secularizing the Faith (1992) followed Protestant clergy through a crisis of belief to the 1920s as “an era of drift”. Their critics attacked this as the secularization thesis. Michael Gauvreau’s The Evangelical Century (1991) argued that the evangelical creed adapted to Darwinism and higher criticism; Marshall replied in 1993–94 that attempts to dismiss secularization were premature. In A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996) Nancy Christie and Gauvreau argued that the Protestant churches reached their greatest cultural influence before 1940 and placed secularization after the Second World War. Behind the debate stands Richard Allen’s The Social Passion (1971), which made the social gospel central to the history of reform, though recent doctoral work cites it far less. Social histories of Protestant culture, Methodism, gender and leisure (Westfall, Semple, Marks) moved the question from doctrine to lay practice. Catholic history developed alongside: Hamelin and Gagnon’s synthesis of Quebec Catholicism, Perin on Rome, McGowan on Irish Toronto. Gauvreau later carried the revision into Quebec, tracing the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action (2005). Later work studies irreligion in settler British Columbia (Marks 2017), distinguishes political from social secularization (Van Die) and treats religion as a vehicle of the liberal order (Christie). Moral reform as regulation belongs to a neighbouring field.
node.scope_note: A research field containing a debate. “Secularization thesis” is the name its critics gave to Cook’s and Marshall’s accounts (Laverdure’s 1998 review of Christie and Gauvreau); Marshall defended the concept in 1993–94. Both sides appear as historians. Catholic and Protestant histories have different genealogies; Irish Catholic history (McGowan, Perin) stays here. The Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution (Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau 2005) has its main home in quebec_historiography, reached from here by the contribution edge crr_rel_04. Moral reform as regulation (Valverde) is placed in moral_regulation.

node.label: Liberal order framework

node.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · coverage through 2000; mostly post-2000 extension

node.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures, and Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
node.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Bannister, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).

representative_people.name: Ian McKay
representative_people.context: Proposes the framework: Canada as a project of liberal rule and liberal hegemony; in his 2009 reply holds that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated; continues it through a history of the Canadian left as a counter-project.
representative_people.works: “The Liberal Order Framework” (2000); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009); Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008)

representative_people.name: Bruce Curtis
representative_people.context: Historical sociologist of state formation through schooling, inspection and the census; Christie credits him with recasting the liberal order as governmentality. A root of the framework, not a follower of it.
representative_people.works: Building the Educational State (1988); True Government by Choice Men? (1992); The Politics of Population (2001); “After ‘Canada’” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012)

representative_people.name: Allan Greer
representative_people.context: Studies a feudal, largely self-sufficient habitant society in rural Quebec before 1840; coedits the state-formation collection Colonial Leviathan; later work on commons, enclosure and "property formation" carries the questions toward property and dispossession.
representative_people.works: Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Colonial Leviathan (1992), ed. with Ian Radforth; “Commons and Enclosure” (2012); Property and Dispossession (2018)

representative_people.name: Ian Radforth
representative_people.context: Coeditor of Colonial Leviathan; primary placement in English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history.
representative_people.works: Colonial Leviathan (1992), ed. with Allan Greer

representative_people.name: Fernande Roy
representative_people.context: Her study of Montreal's francophone business liberalism is named by Pâquet as one of the prospectus's two explicit sources, with Gramsci.
representative_people.works: Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988)

representative_people.name: Michel Ducharme
representative_people.context: Coedits the debate volume; his intellectual history of liberty in the two Canadas distinguishes republican and "modern" liberty before 1838.

representative_people.name: Jean-François Constant

strands.title: The prospectus: Canada as a project of liberal rule

strands.title: Property, market society and capitalism
strands.focus: The editorial reason for separating this entry from moral regulation: the framework's individual is a property-holder, and its later work runs to land, enclosure and taxation. McKay distinguishes liberal order from capitalism; Palmer replies that the distinction lets historians avoid capitalism.
strands.works: McKay, “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009); Weaver, The Great Land Rush (2003); Greer, “Commons and Enclosure” (2012) and Property and Dispossession (2018); Heaman, Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017)

strands.title: Debating the Canadian liberal revolution
strands.focus: The 2009 volume tests the framework across rights, municipalities, conservation, the family, women and racialized people, First Nations and British Columbia; McKay replies with a long liberal revolution of the 1840s–1940s.

strands.title: Critiques
strands.focus: Loyalism rather than liberalism before 1840 (Bannister); a-liberal families (Sandwell); religion, gender and governmentality (Christie); capitalism avoided (Palmer); an unstable definition (Fecteau); thin primary evidence (Ajzenstat).
strands.works: Sandwell (2003, 2009); Bannister (2009); the Underhill Review round table (2009): Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet; Palmer (2009)

strands.title: The left as counter-project

node.description: Studies how morality, sexuality, health and conduct were made objects of governance by reformers, churches, professions, courts and the state, and how regulation shaped the selves of the regulated. The concept came into historical sociology through Philip Corrigan's work (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch (1985), which treated English state formation as a cultural revolution; Ruonavaara describes their framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with Marxist theory. In Canada, Mariana Valverde and Lorna Weir offered preliminary remarks on moral regulation in Resources for Feminist Research (1988), and Valverde's The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) argued that Protestant social-purity reformers were not simply repressive and that they linked sexual health to racial purity and slum clearance. Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987), and later The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Gentile), examined sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians. Studies of contraception and eugenics (McLaren), women, girls and the law (Backhouse, Lévesque, Dubinsky, Strange, Sangster), welfare and single mothers (Little), and postwar normality (Adams, Gleason) widened the field. Adams tied moral regulation to state formation through venereal-disease policy, and Strange and Loo surveyed law and moral regulation from 1867 to 1939 (1997). Critics reformulated the concept: Dean (1994) recast Corrigan's account through Foucault's governmentality, and Ruonavaara (1997) rejected a monolithic, state-only project. The liberal order framework (McKay 2000) is a separate entry, closer to a history of capitalism.
node.scope_note: A research field, international in its theory and Canadian in most of its historical work. The liberal order framework is a separate project, 'closer to history of capitalism' (user, 2026-10-12); state formation (Curtis) is shared ground, not membership. Feminist legal and sexual history overlaps cdn_women_gender; youth and normality overlaps cdn_childhood_youth. Roster inclusion does not mean a scholar adopts the moral-regulation framework.

node.label: Canadian working-class history
node.period_rationale: Period 2 (c. 1970–85) is the formation of the new labour history: Copp 1974, Labour/Le Travailleur 1976, Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980, the 1981 exchange. Logan 1948 is an earlier institutional root; gender, Quebec and welfare-state work continue in period 3.

date_span.basis: Selected publication and institutional milestones. 1948 is an earlier institutional history, not the field’s origin; 1976 is the journal’s first volume (journal archive and Crossref; Freeman 2002 on the founding); 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

node.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
node.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) have their primary placement in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his primary placement is liberal_order_framework.

node.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
node.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in quebec_historiography, where 91% of its citing PhDs sit; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to quebec_historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) have primary placements in native_newcomer and settler_colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with moral_regulation; childhood and family with cdn_childhood_youth. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in cdn_working_class, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (extension).
strands.works: Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Prentice, “Laying Siege to the History Professoriate” (1997); Cleverdon (1950); Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018)

strands.title: Gender history and women's history: the dichotomies exchange
strands.focus: Whether gender history extends or displaces women’s history. Pierson’s 1991 essay opens on the turn to deconstruction and Scott. Sangster’s “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995), by her own later account, protested “the hierarchy being established between a superior gender history and a ‘limited’ women’s history”; replies by Dubinsky and Marks and by Iacovetta and Kealey defended gender history against her dichotomy, and she answered (1996). node.description: Studies children, adolescents and families in Canadian history, and the reformers, experts, courts, schools and welfare programmes that sought to shape them. Neil Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) traced the reformers who pursued social improvement through children. Parr's study of British child immigrants (1980) and her collection Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982), Rooke and Schnell's history of child rescue and the welfare state (1983) and Bradbury's family economies of industrial Montreal (1993) tied the field to family and labour history. The 1990s brought studies of maternal and infant welfare (Comacchio 1993), the baby boom (Owram 1996), youth and the making of heterosexuality (Adams 1997) and psychology and the 'normal' family (Gleason 1999). Francophone work examined family allowances and compulsory schooling (Marshall 1998), juvenile reform schools (Ménard 2003) and the medicalization of motherhood (Baillargeon 2004). Comacchio treats adolescence as a sociohistorical construction (2006); Myers studies girls, the courts and the policing of children in Montreal and beyond (2006, 2019). John Bullen's review essay on recent approaches to child-welfare history (1985) is the one early critique found. Historians also ask how young people's own experience can be recovered: Sutherland on adult memories of childhood (1992), and Gleason's critique of 'agency traps' (2016). The field overlaps with women's and gender history and with moral regulation; residential schooling of Indigenous children is treated primarily in the Native–newcomer entry.
node.scope_note: A research field defined by its topic (the user's 'topic field', 2026-10-12; entry_type follows the atlas vocabulary). It combines histories of children, youth and family with histories of child welfare, health, schooling and juvenile justice. node.label: Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada
node.period_rationale: Selected milestones expand from 1976–83 (Walker, Ward, Avery, Abella and Troper, Perin), i.e. 'Reorientations, c. 1970–85', and continue into period_3 (Anderson 1991, Iacovetta 1992, Walker 1997, Backhouse 1999). Trudel (1960) and Winks (1971) are earlier witnesses. Matches groups.json (period_2/period_3). The Quebec immigration strand adds Taschereau and Anctil (1988) and Pâquet (1997) in period; Pâquet 2005 is extension.

node.description: Studies immigration, ethnic communities, racism and the state in Canada: immigrant workers and their reception, ethnic identity, and the legal and spatial making of racial categories. Earlier works on slavery in New France (Trudel 1960) and on Black Canadians (Winks 1971) preceded an expansion from the mid-1970s. Walker's The Black Loyalists (1976) placed Black community at the centre; Ward's White Canada Forever (1978) traced west-coast prejudice against Asian residents and the discriminatory policies it produced; Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) examined European immigrant workers and labour radicalism; Abella and Troper studied Canada and the Jews of Europe, 1933–48 (1982). Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) asked whether ethnic groups had been 'discovered' just when the state faced challenges such as Quebec nationalism. Studies of Toronto neighbourhoods (Harney, who co-founded the Multicultural History Society of Ontario in 1976), Italian migrants in Montreal (Ramirez), Chinese Montrealers (Helly), Quebec's immigration policy (Pâquet 1997), British Columbia politicians (Roy), Italian immigrants in postwar Toronto (Iacovetta) and Ukrainian-Canadian women (Swyripa) followed. Anderson (1987, 1991) treated 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' as racial categories made through government practice and place, which a reviewer saw as moving beyond earlier studies of white prejudice; Backhouse's Colour-Coded (1999) traced racism through law. Walker distinguished five orientations in African-Canadian historiography, from Black 'clients' of white philanthropy to Black community and 'survivors' (1997). Post-2000 work turned to Cold War reception and citizenship (Iacovetta 2006; Bohaker and Iacovetta 2009).
node.scope_note: A research field joining immigration and ethnic history with histories of racism and Black Canadian history. Black Canadian history is included here as a strand because the request listed no separate entry (see open questions); it is not a subfield of immigration history. Indigenous–settler relations are in native_newcomer and settler_colonialism. Roster inclusion is not adoption of one framework: Ward's 'attitudes and public policy' and Anderson's 'racial category' approaches differ. A reviewer saw Anderson moving beyond earlier studies of white attitudes and prejudice (Stanley 1993); no checked text has Anderson distancing herself from White Canada Forever by name, so she is not listed as Ward's critic.

node.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
node.period_rationale: Period 2 (c. 1970–85) is when the field takes shape: Ray 1974, Trigger 1976 and 1985, Van Kirk and Brown 1980, Delâge 1985. Innis 1930 and Stanley 1936 are earlier resources, not origins; syntheses, schools, health and labour studies continue through period 3.
node.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones. 1930 and 1936 are earlier works the field reworks, not its origin; 1974–85 is the field’s formation; 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary, not an end.

node.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
node.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework and do not adopt it, and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with settler_colonialism.

strands.title: The fur trade in national history

strands.focus: Trigger joins archaeology and documents to Wendat/Huron history before and after contact (1976) and reconsiders the ‘heroic age’ of New France (1985). strands.title: How historians wrote about Indigenous peoples
strands.focus: Walker (1971) and Trigger (1986) survey Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples. Trigger dates such studies from 1971 and describes ethnohistorical work across disciplines moving into national history.

strands.focus: Miller’s national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’ (1989), Dickason’s history of First Nations (1992), and regional or biographical studies (Smith 1987; Coates 1991). strands.title: Agency as alibi? An internal critique
strands.focus: Brownlie and Kelm (1994) criticised agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin 1990; Miller; Loo 1992): stressing Native agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence, trivialising the harm of colonial policy and serving as an ‘alibi’ for it. A critique within policy history, not of the fur-trade literature; targets known from a secondary source, essay unread.
strands.works: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?” CHR 75:4 (December 1994): 543–56

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. Konishi records Indigenous scholars’ critiques of settler colonial studies. Extension only.
strands.works: Greer, “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (JCHA 2019); Konishi (2019)

node.label: Quebec historiography
node.period_rationale: Period 1 (c. 1945–70) is when Quebec historiography professionalizes into university schools: the IHAF (1946) and RHAF (1947), the Montreal and Laval schools in the 1950s–60s. Groulx’s earlier national history is an earlier root in period 0; he is cited by 29 PhDs (2009–26), mostly for his memoirs, as a source. The modernist generation and its critics belong to periods 2 and 3.
node.date_label: Earlier national history (Groulx) · Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française founded 1946, its Revue from 1947 · Montreal and Laval schools 1950s–60s · Histoire du Québec contemporain 1979 · Rudin’s critique 1992 · coverage through 2000; post-2000 extension partial (Catholic Action revision 2002–05)

date_span.basis: Selected milestones. Groulx’s national history is an earlier root, not a boundary; 1946 is the founding of the IHAF and 1947 the Revue’s first issue, not founding dates for the field; 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

node.description: Historical writing on Quebec and French Canada, mostly in French, long organized around the nation, the Conquest of 1760 and the meaning of modernity. Lionel Groulx’s national history of French Canada closes what a francophone anthology calls the time of the ‘ancients’; Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française (1946) and its Revue (1947). In the 1950s historians at Montréal (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) made the Conquest and its consequences their central problem. At Laval, Trudel wrote the history of New France, and Hamelin and Ouellet economic and social history, Ouellet in a conjunctural idiom indebted to Labrousse. Their agricultural-crisis thesis (1962) was contested by Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Dechêne, trained in the Annales milieu in France, wrote the social history of seventeenth-century Montreal (1974). After 1970 a modernist generation turned to contemporary, urban and industrial Quebec and to its whole population (Linteau, Durocher and Robert, 1979). Women’s history followed, from the Collectif Clio (1982) to Baillargeon (1991); Lévesque (1997) asked how far colleagues had integrated it. Behiels (1985) found the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60; Rouillard (1997) recorded a shift from reading it as rupture to turn. Ronald Rudin (1992, 1997) argued that the modernists’ search for a ‘normal’ society muted religion, rurality and ethnicity; Linteau and Fecteau replied (1995). Bouchard and Lamonde (2000) close the period; after 2000, Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue and Gauvreau traced the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action.
node.scope_note: A research field defined by its object (Quebec and French Canada) and largely by its language. The Montreal school, Laval, the modernists and their critics are distinct and overlapping positions, not one school; Savard warns against treating ‘École de Québec’ as a unit. The post-1970 generation is called ‘modernist’ after Bédard and Goyette’s part title; Linteau calls it a ‘nouvelle histoire’; Rudin’s polemical name for it is used only in the normal-society debate strand. Annales influence is indirect and contested: Ouellet’s Labroussian economic history, Mandrou’s preface and Dechêne’s training in the Annales milieu are documented, while Linteau says his generation owed more to sociology and American historians. Groulx’s nationalism and clerical politics are historical subjects here, not the atlas’s categories. Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) and the Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution have their primary homes here. English-language historians of Quebec (Behiels, Dickinson, Young, Rudin, Greer) belong to the field. Acadian and francophone-minority historiography outside Quebec is only touched by Martel. New France encounter history with Indigenous peoples is in native_newcomer.

node.label: Canadian military history
node.period_rationale: Period 1 (c. 1945–70) is when official history dominates: Stanley 1954, Stacey 1955–70, Nicholson 1962. Duguid 1938 is an earlier root; war and society (Morton, Copp, Pierson) belongs to periods 2–3 and memory to period 3.
node.date_label: Duguid’s only official volume 1938 · Stacey’s official histories 1955–70 · Nicholson’s replacement CEF history 1962 · Broken Promises 1977 · war-and-society studies 1986–93 · Walker on race and recruitment 1989 · Valour and the Horror broadcast and hearings 1992 · Vance 1997 · coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones and one public controversy (broadcast January 1992, Senate hearings and Ombudsman’s report later that year; documented in a 1994 volume). 1938 is an earlier official history, not the field’s origin; 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

node.description: Canadian military history has three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. Early work was largely official history, published by authority of the Minister of National Defence. Duguid’s official history of the Great War produced only one volume (1938); Nicholson’s Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962) replaced it. Stacey wrote volumes I (1955) and III (1960) of the Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, and his Arms, Men and Governments (1970) made war policy a subject; Stanley’s Canada’s Soldiers (1954) called Canadians ‘an unmilitary people’. Conscription and French-Canadian participation recur, from Armstrong’s Crisis of Quebec (1937) to Granatstein and Hitsman’s Broken Promises (1977) and francophone histories of the 22nd Battalion (Gagnon 1986) and of bilingualism in the forces (Pariseau and Bernier 1987). From the 1980s war-and-society history turned to soldiers, veterans, psychiatry and women: Morton’s military and political histories (1981, 1985), veterans’ return (Morton and Wright 1987), battle exhaustion (Copp and McAndrew 1990) and Pierson on wartime womanhood (1986). Walker (1989) studied the enlistment of visible minorities, and Dempsey Prairie First Nations soldiers (1999). Popular history (Berton’s Vimy, 1986) and the CBC series The Valour and the Horror (1992), which led to Senate hearings and an ombudsman’s report, made military history a major public controversy. Vance’s Death So Noble (1997) treated the Great War as a cultural force in interwar memory. Cook (2002, 2006) showed that the records and narratives of Stacey’s officers were neither neutral nor unbiased.
node.scope_note: A research field with three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. They are not successive stages; official historians also wrote policy history, and war-and-society historians also wrote operations. Popular history (Berton) and public controversy are included as part of the field’s public life, not as academic scholarship. Francophone work on conscription and French-Canadian participation is part of the field and meets Quebec historiography. Several roster people have primary placements elsewhere (Stanley, Granatstein, Copp, Bercuson, Pierson, Vance); they appear for specific works. Imperial, naval and air histories and the Royal Military College tradition are thin in this selection. Critics of militarized memory (McKay and Swift) are after 2000. Black and Japanese-Canadian soldiers appear through Walker (1989, scholarly) and two community and veteran histories (Ruck 1987, Ito 1984). The Valour and the Horror controversy is a strand here, called a major public-history controversy on a contemporary witness (Dick 1993); Carr’s later treatment (CHR 2005) is unread, so it is not called a defining historiographical controversy.

node.description: Research on the Canadian state, its parties, officials, wars and foreign relations, and the national syntheses built from them. Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975), of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) and of the Ottawa mandarins (1982), Whitaker's study of the Liberal party and the state (1977) and Owram's history of the intellectuals who argued for planning and reform (1986) examined how federal power was organized, staffed and justified. Stacey's history of external policies (1977, 1981), Hillmer and Granatstein's Empire to Umpire (1994) and Bothwell's Alliance and Illusion (2007) treated Canada's place in the world. Bothwell, Drummond and English's Canada since 1945 (1981) and Thompson and Seager's Centenary Series volume (1985) offered national syntheses; political biography (Brown on Borden, Bélanger on Laurier, English on Pearson) and Bliss's business history kept leaders and enterprise in view. Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1994) turned to the security state. Buckner's 1993 address, asking historians to restore the settlement colonies to imperial history, led to the British World volume (2006). Chapnick (2000, 2005) questioned the middle-power 'golden age'. Granatstein and Bliss also led the national side of the 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate. Since 2011 the CHA's political history prizes have rewarded a 'new political history' of state, tax and governance: Heaman on taxation (2017), Loo on forced relocation (2019), Bohaker on Anishinaabe governance (2020), and francophone studies of Hydro-Québec (Savard) and cultural policy (Harvey) that are recognized but not yet widely cited.
node.scope_note: A research field for the political, diplomatic and national history of the Canadian state, widened to include the 'new political history' of state, tax and governance (Heaman's subtitle) that the CHA's political history prizes have recognized since they were first listed in 2011; business history and the British World are distinct strands. The debate over national history is a separate entry (who_killed_debate, user decision 2026-10-12): Granatstein's and Bliss's polemics are placed there, their scholarship here; Bliss's primary placement is here, with a debate roster row there (Q73, user decision 2026-10-12). Military history is a separate proposed entry (cdn_military); Stacey and Granatstein are shared, not merged. Francophone political history (Bélanger; Savard and Harvey, recognized by CHA prizes but not yet widely cited) is thin in the PhD corpus; Quebec political history belongs mostly to quebec_historiography. Post-2000 works are a partial extension.

node.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
node.period_rationale: The exchange runs from Bliss (1991–92) to the 2000 reassessments, inside period_3 (c. 1985–2000); its roots (1967, 1969) and the 2009 volume lie outside. groups.json gives period_3, continuing.
node.date_label: Roots: Cook 1967, Careless 1969 · Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' and the JCS replies 1991–92 · Strong-Boag's CHA address 1994 · Granatstein's book 1998 · CHR replies (McKillop, Palmer) and francophone reviews 1998–99 · CHR forum, Buckner, McKay and Osborne 2000 · Dummitt and Dawson 2009 · coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Publication dates of the debate texts. 1967 and 1969 are roots, not the start of the debate; 2009 is a later intervention, not its end.

node.description: A quarrel among English-Canadian historians in the 1990s over whether national history had been lost, taught here as a moment in the profession's view of itself, not as current practice: few recent theses cite its texts. It had two phases. In 1991–92 Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' argued that intense specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country, and asked historians to remember that their subject was Canada. A 'Point-Counterpoint' in the same journal answered him: Gregory Kealey's class history was 'neither privatizing, nor sundering' (1992), and Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented. Strong-Boag's 1994 presidential address answered 'neo-conservative laments' by indicting an old history of white male elites. In 1998 Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? took the charge to a public audience. In the Canadian Historical Review McKillop (1999) argued that Granatstein's narrow national history was itself political legitimation, and Palmer offered a dissident view. Francophone reviewers answered too: Dubuc read a lament for political history; Dumont, an indictment of social historians built on wrong facts about Quebec schooling. It grew from the 'limited identities' of region, culture and class that Cook named (1967) and Careless popularized (1969). In 2000 Létourneau proposed a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions, Cook called identities contingent and multiple, Buckner revisited limited identities, and McKay offered the liberal order framework as a way past the impasse. Dummitt and Dawson (2009) sought to move beyond political-versus-social history.
node.scope_note: A debate entry measured through its texts, not its people, and written as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding rather than current practice: any core debate text is cited by 34 of 1,303 strict 2009–2026 History PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. It has two phases: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies (1991–92), and Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies (1998–99); the 1992 JCS pieces answer Bliss, not Who Killed Canadian History?. Most participants' citations in the PhD corpus come from their other work. Bliss and Granatstein's scholarship is in cdn_political_national; Bliss's primary placement is cdn_political_national; this entry keeps his debate row (Q80, user decision 2026-10-12). The replying fields are proposed as cdn_working_class, cdn_women_gender and cdn_regional. Several replies are characterized by title only (Gregory Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). The exchange among the main protagonists was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the Bulletin d'histoire politique and the CHA Bulletin (1998–99); no francophone reply to Bliss was found. Létourneau's 2000 CHR essay is the francophone voice in the 2000 reassessments. Quebec's own debate over national and political history (the BHP from 1992, Bélanger 1997, later the 2006–07 school programme) ran separately; its checked texts do not cite Bliss or Granatstein, and it is related here only by comparison. Osborne's school-history essay links to history education, which the atlas does not treat as an entry.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Reid (1987); Buckner (1988). Phase one: Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind" (1991–92), answered in the JCS Point-Counterpoint by G. Kealey (1992) and L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag (1992); Strong-Boag, "Contested Space" (1994). Phase two: Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), answered in the CHR by McKillop, "A View from the Trenches" (1999) and Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); Strong-Boag's review (1999); francophone reviews by Dionne (RHAF 1998), Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999) and Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). Reassessments: Létourneau and the CHR forum (2000); Cook, "Identities Are Not Like Hats" (2000); Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000); McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000); Osborne (2000). Later: Dummitt and Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft (2009); Hamilton (2012).

strands.title: Roots: limited identities
strands.focus: Cook's phrase (1967) and Careless's programme (1969) made region, culture and class the frame; Buckner (1988) judged it premature to abandon; Reid (1987) records the first worries about fragmentation. The debate grows out of this, not out of the 1990s alone.

Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada," Canadian Historical Review 50, no. 1 (1969): 1–10.; Phillip A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship: An Atlantic Provinces Perspective," Journal of Canadian Studies 23, no. 1–2 (1988): 177–198.; John G. Reid, "Towards the Elusive Synthesis: The Atlantic Provinces in Recent General Treatments of Canadian History," Acadiensis 16, no. 2 (1987): 107ff.

strands.title: Phase one, 1991–92: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies
strands.focus: Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (JCS 26:4, 1991–92): specialization had displaced older historians' concern with explaining the country (abstract). A 'Point-Counterpoint' in JCS 27:2 (1992) answered him with 'counter-positions … on the centralist views of Canadian history as articulated by Michael Bliss' (MUSE framing): Gregory Kealey defended class analysis as 'neither privatizing, nor sundering'; Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented (both title level). Strong-Boag's 1994 CHA address answered 'neo-conservative laments' (abstract). These pieces predate Who Killed Canadian History? and are not replies to it.

Journal of Canadian Studies 27, no. 2 (1992): 129–131.; Veronica Strong-Boag, "Presidential Address: Contested Space: The Politics of Canadian Memory," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association 5, no. 1 (1994): 3–17.

strands.title: Phase two, 1998–99: Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies
strands.focus: Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), which named the debate, took the charge to a public audience (as McKillop summarizes it: academic historians had abandoned a national past for 'overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history'). In the CHR McKillop (80:2, June 1999) argued that Granatstein miscasts the scholar as citizen and that his national history is itself political legitimation; Palmer (80:4, December 1999) offered 'a dissident view' (title level). Strong-Boag reviewed the book in Historical Studies in Education (1999; unread). Francophone historians answered the book too, as reviewers: Dionne in RHAF (1998); Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc in the BHP (1999), Dubuc reading it as a lament for political history as a discipline (first page); and Dumont in the CHA Bulletin (1999, read in full), who corrected its claims about Quebec schooling and called it a fierce indictment of social historians. No francophone reply to Bliss was found.

strands.title: Reassessments of 2000
strands.focus: The CHR forum on Létourneau's call for a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions (respondents include Cook, Valverde, Miller, Owram, Tillotson, Palmer, Iacovetta, Mitchinson); Cook on contingent, multiple identities; Buckner revisiting limited identities; McKay's liberal order as an exit from the impasse; Osborne on school history.

strands.focus: Contesting Clio's Craft (2009) seeks to move past political-versus-social history through transnational and comparative approaches; Palmer's review finds old debates "at times … misrepresented"; Hamilton (2012) finds most Journal of Canadian Studies contributors of 1999–2009 adopted limited identities.

node.label: Canadian regional history
node.period_rationale: Provincial syntheses (Morton 1957, Ormsby 1958) and the limited-identities argument (1967, 1969) fall in period_1; Acadiensis (1971) and the regional syntheses of the 1970s–90s carry the field into period_2 and period_3. groups.json gives period_1/period_2.
node.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000 · coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Selected milestones; provincial and local history is much older. Engagement in 2009–2026 PhDs is steady.

node.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. In 1971 Buckner founded Acadiensis, complaining that historians remained 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen's The Canadian Prairies (1984), Barman's The West Beyond the West (1991), Conrad and Hiller's Atlantic Canada (2001) and Waiser's Saskatchewan (2005) offered regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.
node.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in native_newcomer, settler_colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

representative_people.name: W. L. Morton
representative_people.context: Historian of Manitoba and the West; his provincial synthesis (1957) precedes the limited-identities argument. In 1946 he asked on what premises the established national interpretations rested (abstract).
representative_people.works: Manitoba: A History (1957); "Clio in Canada" (1946)

representative_people.name: Margaret A. Ormsby
representative_people.context: Author of the centennial history of British Columbia (1958), which Barman later called "an invaluable beginning point" (as reported in BC Studies). Reimer's history of BC historical writing ends in 1958, the province's centenary and the year of her book, and treats her with W. Kaye Lamb as a first generation of BC historians (contents; Favrholdt's review). President of the Canadian Historical Association in 1965–66, its second woman president after Hilda Neatby (1962–63) (CHA list).
representative_people.works: British Columbia: A History (1958)

representative_people.name: Ramsay Cook
representative_people.context: Suggested in 1967 that Canadianism might be found in "the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have" (quoted by Buckner). Primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.
representative_people.works: "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967)

representative_people.name: J. M. S. Careless
representative_people.context: Made "limited identities of region, culture and class" a programme for Canadian history (1969, via Buckner's quotations); later synthesized regions, cities and identities before 1914 (1989).
representative_people.works: "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Frontier and Metropolis (1989)

representative_people.name: Phillip Buckner
representative_people.context: Founded Acadiensis (1971) against historians "obsessed with the great 'national' themes"; defended limited identities from an Atlantic perspective (1988) and revisited the concept (2000). Primary placement proposed in cdn_political_national.
representative_people.works: "Acadiensis II" (1971); "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship" (1988); "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000)

representative_people.name: T. W. Acheson
representative_people.context: Traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy tariff and its subordination to Montreal capital in the 1890s (1972, opening read).
representative_people.works: "The National Policy and the Industrialization of the Maritimes, 1880–1910" (1972)

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001) is a francophone university synthesis of Maritime Acadia over four centuries that sets out to recount the experience of the whole Acadian people, not only its elite. Most of these works are post-2000 (partial extension). Readers of this literature also engage Quebec historiography (lift 3.2): see the comparison with quebec_historiography.

node.label: Canada’s 1960s
node.period_rationale: Extension entry (period null). Inside 1920–2000 are early accounts (Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984), the Quiet Revolution's origins (Behiels 1985), Gélinas (1996), Martel (1997) and Owram (1996). The field's consolidation (Igartua 2006 to Milligan 2014) is post-2000.
node.date_label: Early accounts: Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984 · Behiels 1985 · Owram 1996 · Igartua 2006 · Palmer, Warren 2008–09 · Mills 2010 · Debating Dissent 2012 · coverage through 2000; mostly post-2000 extension

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. Participants' and journalists' writing on the decade began earlier; 1980 is the first selected book and 2020 the latest. Neither bounds the field.

node.description: Historical writing that treats Canada's long 1960s as a subject in its own right: the baby boom and youth revolt, the New Left and labour militancy, Quebec's Quiet Revolution and its radicalisms, rights movements, decolonization and Red Power, and the remaking of national identity. Book-length accounts began with Kostash's interview-based history of her own generation (1980) and Levitt (1984). Doug Owram's Born at the Right Time (1996) followed the baby-boom generation from suburb and school to counterculture and youth radicalism. José Igartua's The Other Quiet Revolution (2006) traced English Canada's British self-definition giving way to a civic, rights-based identity, and Dominique Clément studied its rights associations. Bryan Palmer's Canada's 1960s (2009) read the decade through the ironies of national identity, with chapters on wildcat strikes, the New Left, Quebec and the 'discovery' of the 'Indian'. Sean Mills's The Empire Within (2010) traced postcolonial thought in Montreal activism, and David Austin race, sex and security there. Campbell, Clément and Kealey's Debating Dissent (2012) and Ian Milligan's Rebel Youth (2014), on young workers and New Leftists, widened the field. Francophone historians debate continuity and rupture. Michael Behiels, E.-Martin Meunier and Jean-Philippe Warren, and Louise Bienvenue found the Quiet Revolution's roots in postwar liberalism and in Catholic Action, against its own story of a 'grande noirceur'. Warren's Une douce anarchie (2008) historicized the student revolt of 1968. It is a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram, Palmer, Mills, Igartua), not a school like the atlas's New Left entry.
node.scope_note: A research field defined by its subject, the long 1960s (roughly late 1950s to early 1970s), not by a method or school. It replaces the "postwar Canada" data cluster (user, 2026-10-12: "1960s is its own thing"). Distinguish the atlas's New Left entry (radical historians as a school) from histories of the New Left as a movement. The Quebec strand overlaps Quebec historiography and the Catholic Action revision in religion history; those works keep their primary placements there. Register (answers Q94): a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram 71 and Palmer 67 citing PhDs; Mills; Igartua), with engagement modestly falling (ratio 0.78; fixed panel 0.81), not a school. Black Canadian sixties history: Austin (2013) covers the post-2000 extension; before 2000 the only verified work is a contemporary participants' collection (Forsythe, ed., 1971), so pre-2000 scholarly coverage is a gap.

node.label: Settler colonialism
node.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999, 2006 · Veracini 2010 · journal 2011 · selected critiques 2013–20; field chronology unresolved

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1983 and 1995 are earlier settler-society witnesses, not the field's origin; Wolfe 1999 is the only selected milestone inside 1920–2000. Naming and consolidation fall after 2000; neither endpoint bounds the field.

node.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
node.scope_note: A selective research-field draft, mostly in the partial post-2000 extension. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.
