strands.title: Structure, not event
strands.focus: Wolfe's account treats invasion and elimination as a continuing structure. Kauanui's abstract attests the formulation and its critique; Wolfe's own pages are not checked here.
strands.works: Patrick Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (London and New York: Cassell, 1999). Writing Past Colonialism series.; Patrick Wolfe, "Land, Labor, and Difference: Elementary Structures of Race," American Historical Review 106, no. 3 (2001): 866–905.; Patrick Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native," Journal of Genocide Research 8, no. 4 (2006): 387–409.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).

strands.title: Settler colonial theory and field formation
strands.focus: Veracini disentangles settler colonial from colonial phenomena and introduces a dedicated journal (2011); a 2013 essay traces the concept's earlier career. Field-making, not a claim of single origin.
strands.works: Lorenzo Veracini, "Settler Collective, Founding Violence and Disavowal: The Settler Colonial Situation," Journal of Intercultural Studies 29, no. 4 (2008): 363–379.; Lorenzo Veracini, Settler Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010).; Lorenzo Veracini, "Introducing: Settler Colonial Studies," Settler Colonial Studies 1, no. 1 (2011): 1–12.; Lorenzo Veracini, "'Settler Colonialism': Career of a Concept," Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 41, no. 2 (2013): 313–333.; Edward Cavanagh and Lorenzo Veracini, eds., The Routledge Handbook of the History of Settler Colonialism (London: Routledge, 2017).

strands.title: Settler capitalism and settler societies before the name
strands.focus: Comparative settler economies (1983) and gender, race, ethnicity and class in settler societies (1995) precede the paradigm's consolidation; Veracini's history of the concept records decolonization-era usage.
strands.works: Donald Denoon, Settler Capitalism: The Dynamics of Dependent Development in the Southern Hemisphere (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1983).; Daiva Stasiulis and Nira Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies: Articulations of Gender, Race, Ethnicity and Class (London: SAGE, 1995).; Lorenzo Veracini, "'Settler Colonialism': Career of a Concept," Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 41, no. 2 (2013): 313–333.

strands.title: Comparative and twentieth-century settler colonies
strands.focus: Comparative collections and studies beyond the British settler dominions, including African settler and native political identities.
strands.works: Caroline Elkins and Susan Pedersen, eds., Settler Colonialism in the Twentieth Century: Projects, Practices, Legacies (New York: Routledge, 2005).; Mahmood Mamdani, "Beyond Settler and Native as Political Identities: Overcoming the Political Legacy of Colonialism," Comparative Studies in Society and History 43, no. 4 (2001): 651–664.; Mahmood Mamdani, Neither Settler nor Native: The Making and Unmaking of Permanent Minorities (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2020).

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence
strands.focus: Indigenous political theory read alongside the paradigm. These works have their own genealogies in Indigenous thought and are not a subset of settler-colonial studies. Open question: these may belong in Indigenous history instead.
strands.works: Glen Sean Coulthard, Red Skin, White Masks: Rejecting the Colonial Politics of Recognition (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2014). Foreword by Taiaiake Alfred.; Audra Simpson, Mohawk Interruptus: Political Life Across the Borders of Settler States (Durham: Duke University Press, 2014).; Leanne Simpson [Leanne Betasamosake Simpson], Dancing on Our Turtle's Back: Stories of Nishnaabeg Re-Creation, Resurgence and a New Emergence (Winnipeg: Arbeiter Ring, 2011).; Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, As We Have Always Done: Indigenous Freedom through Radical Resistance (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2017).; Jodi A. Byrd, The Transit of Empire: Indigenous Critiques of Colonialism (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2011).; Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang, "Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 1, no. 1 (2012).

strands.title: Dispossession, reserves and colonial geography in Canada
strands.focus: Harris explains reserve-making as geographical dispossession, backed by state power, capital and settlers, and later reflects on the framework's boundaries. Carter's prairie reserve agriculture predates the paradigm.
strands.works: Cole Harris, The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change (Vancouver: UBC Press, 1997).; Cole Harris, Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2002).; Cole Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire," Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94, no. 1 (2004): 165–182.; Cole Harris, A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2020).; Sarah Carter, Lost Harvests: Prairie Indian Reserve Farmers and Government Policy (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 1990).

strands.title: Gender, family and colonial nation-making
strands.focus: Gender, race, marriage and child removal in colonial British Columbia, the Prairie West, the American West and Australia. Metadata level only.
strands.works: Adele Perry, On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2001).; Sarah Carter, The Importance of Being Monogamous: Marriage and Nation Building in Western Canada to 1915 (Edmonton: University of Alberta Press / Athabasca University Press, 2008).; Margaret D. Jacobs, White Mother to a Dark Race: Settler Colonialism, Maternalism, and the Removal of Indigenous Children in the American West and Australia, 1880–1940 (Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 2009).

strands.title: Settler identity, truth telling and reconciliation
strands.focus: Settler self-examination after residential schools and in contemporary Canada; Regan's contents page names the 'peacemaker myth'.
strands.works: Paulette Regan, Unsettling the Settler Within: Indian Residential Schools, Truth Telling, and Reconciliation in Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010). Foreword by Taiaiake Alfred.; Emma Battell Lowman and Adam J. Barker, Settler: Identity and Colonialism in 21st Century Canada (Halifax and Winnipeg: Fernwood, 2015).; Sherene H. Razack, ed., Race, Space, and the Law: Unmapping a White Settler Society (Toronto: Between the Lines, 2002).

strands.title: Health, starvation and state policy
strands.focus: Co-citation places Daschuk's Plains history next to Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58 Wolfe/Veracini-citing PhDs). Its own framing is unchecked, so this is a comparison strand.
strands.works: James Daschuk, Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life (Regina: University of Regina Press, 2013).

strands.title: Labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Integrates settler workers' ongoing appropriation of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Fred Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework: Rethinking Canadian Working-Class History," Labour/Le Travail 83 (2019): 173–197.

strands.title: Critiques: structure, region and period
strands.focus: Structural inevitability (Macoun and Strakosch), a teleology of elimination (Rowse), regional and periodic fit with other modes of colonialism (Greer), universal theory or English heritage (Shoemaker).
strands.works: Alissa Macoun and Elizabeth Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory," Settler Colonial Studies 3, nos. 3–4 (2013): 426–443.; Tim Rowse, "Indigenous Heterogeneity," Australian Historical Studies 45, no. 3 (2014): 297–310.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Empire in Early America," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 383–390.; Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism: Universal Theory or English Heritage?" William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 369–374.; Jeffrey Ostler and Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism in Early American History: Introduction," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 361–368.

strands.title: Indigenous scholars on settler colonial studies
strands.focus: Whether the field recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories.
strands.works: Shino Konishi, "First Nations Scholars, Settler Colonial Studies, and Indigenous History," Australian Historical Studies 50, no. 3 (2019): 285–304.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people.
strands.works: Tapji Garba and Sara-Maria Sorentino, "Slavery Is a Metaphor: A Critical Commentary on Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

relationships.relationship: An English-Canadian instance of national narrative

relationships.relationship: The fragmentation charge against the new social history

relationships.relationship: Limited identities and regional history as the debate's ground

relationships.relationship: National-political history as one side of the debate

relationships.relationship: Parallel debates over national narrative in English Canada and Quebec
relationships.evidence_note: Dumont's review of Who Killed Canadian History? (CHA Bulletin 1999, read in full) joins the two debates: she corrects Granatstein's claims about Quebec schooling, calls his book a fierce indictment of social historians with 'visées politiques', and cites Ferretti's chapter in Comeau and Dionne, eds., À propos de l'histoire nationale (1998), and Létourneau's student surveys. Dionne, who reviewed the book in RHAF (1998; title level), co-edited that volume. Létourneau (CHR 2000, abstract) proposes a narration of Canada that is neither unitarist nor fragmenting. Comparison: concurrent, separate debates linked through a few people, not texts; no checked Quebec-debate text cites Bliss or Granatstein (research Q81), and only 4 strict 2009–2026 PhDs cite texts from both. PhD context: 14 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the quebec_historiography anchor set (41% vs 16% of all; lift 2.63). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relationships.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over what historians owe facts and publics
relationships.evidence_note: McKillop (1999, abstract) answers Granatstein that "event-driven facts are inseparable from considerations of value and therefore from the realm of the interpretive". Comparison only: the Canadian debate was about national history and specialization, not postmodernism; no checked text links it to Jenkins, Evans or Appleby, Hunt and Jacob.

relationships.relationship: A national field within intellectual history
relationships.evidence_note: Titles name the field's objects (Canadian thought, intellectuals and the state, historical writing); Gauvreau's Evangelical Century was presented as transforming "the way Canadian intellectual history is interpreted". Comparison: the Canadian field developed largely apart from the contextualist and conceptual programmes in the atlas entry; no checked source links them.

relationships.relationship: Canadian studies of collective memory, pageantry and the public past
relationships.evidence_note: Vance studies Canada's collective memory of the First World War; Nelles "the politics of memory" at the 1908 tercentenary; McKay and Bates the making of Nova Scotia's public past. A contribution of case studies, not a claim that the field originated memory studies.

relationships.relationship: Ideas and representations of Canadian nationhood
relationships.evidence_note: Berger's chapters on Canada First and "The Canadian Character"; Vance on war memory and Canadian nationalism; Igartua on the shift from ethnic to civic national identity. Comparison: the Canadian works rarely engage the modernist theory debates of the atlas entry in the checked pages.

relationships.relationship: Spectacle, exhibition and representation
relationships.evidence_note: Heaman's "Exhibition Culture" and commodification, Walden's exhibition and urban culture, and Radforth's public spectacle share the new cultural history's attention to representation and performance. Comparison only: no checked page cites the new cultural historians.

relationships.relationship: Tourism, heritage and the making of public pasts
relationships.evidence_note: McKay and Bates trace tourism/history and the cultural politics of whiteness in Nova Scotia; McKay's Quest of the Folk shows the tourism industry refashioning regional identity. These study public history as a subject rather than practising it.

relationships.relationship: Berger's historiography of English-Canadian historical writing
relationships.map_label: Writing the history of Canadian history
relationships.evidence_note: Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976; subtitle "Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970") is the standard analysis of the tradition the proposed national-tradition entry describes (groups.json scope). Title-level evidence only; the book's chapters were not checked. Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: Religious thought and social criticism
relationships.evidence_note: Cook's Regenerators belongs to both fields; Gauvreau's Evangelical Century reassesses Cook as intellectual history. PhD context: 34 PhDs engage both drafts (lift 3.5). Both endpoints proposed.

relationships.relationship: Intellectual history answers the liberal order framework
relationships.evidence_note: McNairn's chapter is titled "In Hope and Fear: Intellectual History, Liberalism, and the Liberal Order Framework"; McKay and Heaman write in both fields. PhD context: 43 PhDs engage both drafts (lift 3.5). Title-level only; both endpoints proposed.

relationships.relationship: Postwar national identity and the generation of the 1960s
relationships.evidence_note: Igartua traces English Canada's "other Quiet Revolution" in national identity, 1945–71; Owram moves from intellectuals and the state (1986) to the baby boom (1996). PhD context: 40 PhDs engage both drafts (lift 2.5). Both endpoints proposed.

relationships.relationship: An intellectual historian answers Granatstein
relationships.evidence_note: McKillop argues that Granatstein "miscasts the role of the scholar as citizen" and that his narrow national history is itself political legitimation. One contributor's intervention, not the whole field's position. Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: English-Canadian and Quebec histories of ideas and commemoration
relationships.evidence_note: Lamonde's histoire sociale des idées is Quebec's counterpart; Nelles studies Quebec's tercentenary and Coates and Morgan Madeleine de Verchères. PhD context: 16 of 27 PhDs citing Lamonde (2000) are at francophone universities, against 2 of 48 for Berger (1976). Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: War memory as cultural history
relationships.evidence_note: Vance's Death So Noble "deals with cultural history more than military history" while treating the war's memory. Comparison only; target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: Race as a historically made category
relationships.map_label: Racial formation and Canadian race history
relationships.evidence_note: Anderson (1987, abstract read) treats racial categories as cultural ascriptions whose construction cannot be taken for granted and shows government inscribing 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' in practice and space; racial formation treats race as historically specific and produced through social and political relations. Parallel, not derivation: PhD context shows Omi or Winant cited by 1 of 172 PhDs engaging this group (and by 7 of 1303 overall).

relationships.relationship: African-Canadian historiography
relationships.evidence_note: Walker's 1997 essay (full text read) identifies five orientations in African-Canadian historiography by the role they assign to Black people (Clients, Victims, Achievers, Community, Survivors), and dates the Community orientation to the social-history movement and his own Black Loyalists (1976). Winks (1971) and Trudel (1960) are earlier works. A Canadian contribution to Black history; it does not make Black history a subfield of immigration history.

relationships.relationship: Ethnicity, recognition and the politics of its discovery
relationships.evidence_note: Perin's opening asks whether it is coincidence that ethnic groups were 'discovered' when the US faced the civil rights movement and Canada an assertive Quebec nationalism. The identity umbrella groups historical recovery with struggles over exclusion and recognition and is itself open to criticism. Comparison; Perin's full argument was not read.

relationships.relationship: Immigrant workers and labour radicalism
relationships.evidence_note: Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979; reviewed by Bruno Ramirez in International Labor and Working-Class History) and Ramirez's On the Move (1991) study immigrant workers; Iacovetta's 'Manly Militants' (1995) reviews how historians wrote about immigrants (title-level). PhD context: 97 of 142 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_immigration_ethnicity also engage cdn_working_class (68%; lift 3.37), counted after removing shared anchors (Palmer). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relationships.relationship: Immigrant, ethnic and racialized women
relationships.evidence_note: Iacovetta (1992), Swyripa (1993) and Epp, Iacovetta and Swyripa, eds., Sisters or Strangers? (2004) work at the meeting of the two fields. Title-level. PhD context: 94 of 133 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_immigration_ethnicity also engage cdn_women_gender (71%; lift 2.98), counted after removing shared anchors (Iacovetta). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relationships.relationship: Citizenship programmes for newcomers and Indigenous peoples
relationships.evidence_note: Bohaker and Iacovetta (abstract read) show that from 1950 to 1966 the Indian Affairs branch sat in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and modelled its activities on citizenship campaigns for immigrants. A post-2000 comparison across the two fields. PhD context: 74 of 172 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_immigration_ethnicity also engage native_newcomer (43%; lift 2.3), counted after removing shared anchors. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relationships.relationship: Religious thought as Canadian intellectual history
relationships.evidence_note: Gauvreau's Evangelical Century treats the evangelical creed as "the intellectual expression" of Protestant culture and was presented as transforming how Canadian intellectual history is read; Marshall's summary calls secularization "a key development in Canadian religious and intellectual history". Comparison: much of the field is social rather than intellectual history.

relationships.relationship: Social-history methods turn the field toward lay practice
relationships.evidence_note: Marks studies church and leisure participation by class and gender in three Ontario towns; Christie and Gauvreau subtitle their 2010 synthesis "A Social History of Religion in Canada". Neither names the new social history as a source; the contribution is of method and subject, not an influence claim.

relationships.relationship: Catholic Action revisionism reinterprets the Quiet Revolution
relationships.map_label: Catholic origins of the Quiet Revolution
relationships.evidence_note: Gauvreau's review: Quebec religious history had repeated "the conventional ideology of the Quiet Revolution" until Catholic Action studies shifted attention to laypeople; Baum sets out the social-democratic (Meunier and Warren) and family-and-gender (Gauvreau) versions. PhD context: 16 of the 47 PhDs citing Gauvreau (2005) and 14 of 22 citing Bienvenue are at francophone universities. Target is proposed.
relationships.coordination: Kept after the Catholic Action strand moved to quebec_historiography (answer to Q12): the contribution now runs from Gauvreau’s home field to the strand quebec_historiography/catholic_action_origins. The quebec_historiography draft keeps its broad comparison qcreq_rel_06; the atlas allows the two to coexist (cf. edge_041/edge_369).

relationships.relationship: Religious continuities behind the 1960s
relationships.evidence_note: Hébert: monographs on pre-1960 youth movements (including Bienvenue and Gauvreau) sought to refute the idea that before '68 there was no salvation. Baum: Gauvreau carries Catholic Action's values into 1960s marriage and the refusal of Humanae vitae (1968). Shared works inflate the PhD overlap between the two drafts (lift 4.2), so it is not cited as evidence. Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: Gender, family and religious life
relationships.evidence_note: Marks's chapters on church ladies, freethinkers and working-class women in the Salvation Army; Gauvreau on Catholic Action, the family and women's desire (per Baum); Households of Faith on separate spheres, masculinity, fatherhood and personalist feminism. Comparison only; target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: Religion as a vehicle of the liberal order
relationships.evidence_note: Christie: work on the Protestant churches and New Liberalism means no one "can ignore religion as a powerful vehicle in the creation of the liberal order"; the Catholic church also articulated liberal values. She offers this as an extension that also criticizes McKay's neglect of religion. Van Die's political versus social secularization is set within the "liberal state"; Christie's Households of Faith (2001) opens with "the Rise of Liberal Society" and closes on "Canada’s Liberal Tradition", before McKay's framework was debated. Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: National and Quebec syntheses of women's history
relationships.evidence_note: The atlas's women entry groups national and regional syntheses (French, German, Nigerian) in a strand with different scopes and documentary bases. The Collectif Clio's Quebec synthesis (1982), which rejects a male-centred collective history, and Prentice et al.'s survey (1988) can be read alongside them. Comparison, not descent: Canadian women's history is not presented as a branch of any one national model.

relationships.relationship: Canadian debates over gender as a category
relationships.evidence_note: Pierson's 1991 essay opens on feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis, naming Scott's theory of gender as the most acclaimed example. Parr (1995) and the 1995–96 Left History exchange (Sangster; Iacovetta and Kealey; Dubinsky and Marks) argued over gender history and women's history; their citations are checked, and Sangster's own position is taken from her 2011 retrospect; the replies are read only as defences of gender history. PhD context: 64 of 328 PhDs engaging this group cite Scott (20% vs 9% of all; lift 2.12).

relationships.relationship: Women's history questions a male-centred Quebec history
relationships.evidence_note: The Collectif Clio's introduction argues that a history centred on male figures had been presented as the collective history of the whole population. Lévesque's 1997 assessment says women's history redefined traditional Quebec history and hopes the slowness of some colleagues to integrate women is a matter of time and generation. A specific critique of how Quebec historiography treated women, not a rejection of that historiography. Coexists with qcreq_rel_07 (comparison) in drafts/quebec_historiography: a broad comparison and this specific critique can stand together, as GRAPH-FORMAT.md allows. Kept after Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) was made primary in quebec_historiography (Q38).

relationships.relationship: Gender as a dimension of class and family economies
relationships.evidence_note: Parr's comparison of a textile town where most wage earners were women with a furniture town challenges conventional views of the distinctiveness of gender and class roles (author's book page). Bradbury's Working Families (age, gender and family survival) and Sangster's Dreams of Equality (women on the left) are title-level. Contribution of gender analysis to labour history; it does not claim the new labour history lacked it entirely. PhD context: 130 of 287 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_women_gender also engage cdn_working_class (45%; lift 2.81), counted after removing shared anchors (Bradbury, Parr, Sangster). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.
relationships.review_flag: women and gender history -> working-class history as both contribution (Parr) and critique (Sangster 2000): two claims on one directed pair; the reviewer should keep both or choose one

relationships.relationship: Postwar domestic goods, magazines and households
relationships.evidence_note: Parr's Domestic Goods (1999), Korinek's reading of Chatelaine (2000) and Fahrni's Household Politics (2005) place women and households at the centre of postwar consumption. Title-level only: none of these books was read, so the comparison is a teaching pointer to the consumption entry, not a claim about their arguments.

relationships.relationship: Gramsci's hegemony informs the prospectus
relationships.evidence_note: Pâquet names Gramsci as one of two explicit influences on the prospectus; Ajzenstat describes McKay as recommending "a Gramscian approach"; Palmer argues McKay's reading of Gramscian hegemony is too seamless. McKay's abstract uses "liberal hegemony" and "commonsense". PhD context: 9 of the 91 PhDs citing McKay 2000 also cite a Gramsci work. Influence on the prospectus only, not on every work in the roster.

relationships.relationship: Marxist labour historians charge the framework with avoiding capitalism
relationships.evidence_note: Palmer: as a "seemingly trans-historical analytic framework" liberal order "sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism’s changing historical structures"; historians should name "capitalism as systematic exploitation". One critic's position; it does not speak for all labour historians. Source endpoint is a proposed entry.

relationships.relationship: Liberal order and capitalism: analytically separate, historically entangled
relationships.evidence_note: Fecteau quotes McKay that liberalism and capitalism must be kept "analytically separate" (2000, 629) yet after the 1840s "could not be easily separated" (2009, 385), and quotes McKay in 1994 on a "liberal capitalist order … based on possessive individualism". A teaching comparison between historical-materialist categories and the framework, not a descent.

relationships.relationship: Property, land, taxation and market society
relationships.evidence_note: Weaver relates property rights to the growth of democracy and the market economy; Heaman places "the propertied versus the people" at the centre of Canadian political history; Greer studies property formation. These carry the framework's questions into economic and social history. The atlas has no history-of-capitalism entry; see lof_rel_05.

relationships.relationship: Draws social and political history into a renewed political history
relationships.evidence_note: Parnaby: McKay argued that liberalism as a "project of rule" could draw social and political history into one problematique, and interest in that question has reinvigorated histories of political ideas, institutions, census taking, border making and tax collecting. A contribution, not a claim that it founded political history in Canada.

relationships.relationship: Governmentality as a reading of the liberal order
relationships.evidence_note: Christie cites Curtis's point that what McKay describes is "governmentality", which she finds more precise; Curtis's Ruling by Schooling Quebec is subtitled "Conquest to Liberal Governmentality". The contribution runs through Curtis; whether McKay drew on Foucault directly is unchecked. PhD context: 7 of 91 McKay-citing PhDs cite Foucault's governmentality lectures.

relationships.relationship: Liberal rule and moral regulation: neighbouring, distinct projects
relationships.evidence_note: The user kept them apart (2026-10-12): the framework is "a different project closer to history of capitalism". Pâquet links the framework to studies of "liberal social regulation", and Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender organization. PhD context: 27 of 91 McKay-citing PhDs also cite Valverde (lift 3.6). Comparison only; both endpoints proposed or new.

relationships.relationship: Offers a way past the social versus national-political impasse
relationships.evidence_note: McKay's abstract frames the prospectus as a way past "the present socio-cultural versus national-political impasse in Canadian history writing"; Ajzenstat sets it against Granatstein's attempt to revive national history. An intervention in the debate's terms, not a party to every exchange in it. Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: Family and gender historians question a property-holding individual
relationships.map_label: Families, women and the liberal individual
relationships.evidence_note: Sandwell: a-liberal values persisted in families, "hot zones" where liberal order was imposed, contested or rejected. Christie: McKay's "definition of individualism based on property ownership" excludes women. Perry's chapter title places women and racialized people in its making. Both endpoints are proposed entries.

relationships.relationship: Property formation, land and dispossession
relationships.evidence_note: Greer studies property formation and the dispossession of Indigenous peoples; Weaver the appropriation of land and the emergence of property rights in settler societies; Brownlie's chapter title calls First Nations' relation to the liberal order "a persistent antagonism". Comparison only: no checked source joins the two frameworks.

relationships.relationship: Francophone histories of liberalism and liberty
relationships.evidence_note: Pâquet names Fernande Roy's history of francophone business liberalism as an explicit source of the prospectus; Ducharme's history of liberty in the two Canadas and Fecteau's critique carry the debate in Quebec scholarship. PhD context: Roy (1988) is cited by 16 PhDs, 8 at francophone universities. Target is proposed.

relationships.relationship: State formation as historical sociology
relationships.evidence_note: Curtis presents Ruling by Schooling Quebec as "A Historical Sociology" and Pâquet ties the framework to studies of state formation. Comparison only: no checked source links the Canadian work to the comparative historical sociology the atlas entry describes. Corrigan and Sayer's Great Arch is co-cited (6 of 10 citing PhDs also cite McKay 2000) but unread.

relationships.relationship: A national field within military history
relationships.map_label: Canadian military history and military history
relationships.evidence_note: The atlas’s Military history entry has no Canadian participants. Cook’s account of Stacey and the Army Historical Section (official history as archive-making and narrative) parallels the military entry’s concern with source access and narrative framing. Comparison: the Canadian field is not presented as derived from Howard or Keegan.

relationships.relationship: Great War memory in interwar Canada
relationships.map_label: Vance: memory of the Great War
relationships.evidence_note: Vance’s Death So Noble examines Canada’s collective memory of the Great War in the 1920s and 1930s as a cultural and philosophical force (publisher description). A contribution to the memory entry’s war_mourning strand alongside Winter; no claim that Vance derives from Winter. Cook (2006) extends the question to historians’ own role. PhD context: Death So Noble is cited by 67 PhDs 2009–2026, the most of any work by this roster.

relationships.relationship: Conscription and French-Canadian participation
relationships.evidence_note: Armstrong (1937), Granatstein and Hitsman (1977), Gagnon (1986, 1995) and Pariseau (1987) write conscription and French-Canadian participation; Gagnon’s 1995 essay assesses French-Canadian historians’ treatment of the Second World War in a Bulletin d’histoire politique dossier on ‘myths and realities’. Overlapping subject and venues, different questions. PhD context: 53 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 26.9).

relationships.relationship: Women and war
relationships.map_label: Women and the Second World War
relationships.evidence_note: Pierson’s “They’re Still Women After All”: The Second World War and Canadian Womanhood (1986) belongs to both fields; Pierson anchors the proposed women and gender entry. Title-level.

relationships.relationship: Military history as public argument
relationships.evidence_note: The CBC series The Valour and the Horror aired in January 1992; Senate subcommittee hearings began in late June 1992 and the CBC Ombudsman’s report was released on 10 November 1992. Dick (Archivaria, 1993) says the series ‘prompted unprecedented public reaction and discussion’. Official and academic historians wrote reports for the Ombudsman, collected with an appendix on the RCAF official history in Bercuson and Wise (1994; contents checked). Berton’s popular Vimy (1986) is a second witness. Comparison with the Public history entry; no direction asserted.

relationships.relationship: Foucauldian analysis contributes to the concept of moral regulation and its governmentality reformulation
relationships.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. PhD context: 46 of 107 PhDs citing Valverde 1991 also cite Foucault (43% vs 20% of all PhDs). Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges; an influence edge would need Valverde's own acknowledgement of the debt, which was sought (2026-10-12) but not found in checked text. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

relationships.relationship: State formation as cultural revolution
relationships.map_label: Corrigan and Sayer: The Great Arch
relationships.evidence_note: Ruonavaara: Corrigan and Sayer introduced moral regulation to sociological debate in their historical sociology of English state formation, The Great Arch (1985). Adams applies it to state formation through Ontario VD policy. Corrigan and Sayer are not in the historicalsociology roster; this edge records a contribution from comparative historical sociology, not membership.

relationships.relationship: Sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against queers
relationships.evidence_note: Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987) and Kinsman and Gentile's history of the security campaign that spied on, interrogated and harassed gays and lesbians from the 1950s to the late 1990s (publisher page read) contribute Canadian studies of sexual regulation. Complements the queer entry's regulation strand; it does not claim Canadian priority.

relationships.relationship: Protestant reformers as regulators and as religious actors
relationships.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently; no critique is asserted because the checked texts do not state one. PhD context: 67 of 164 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_religion_reform (41%; lift 3.97), counted after removing shared anchors. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs. [Merged with crr_rel_03 from cdn_religion_reform: Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. PhD context: 25 of 42 PhDs citing The Regenerators also cite Valverde (lift 7.2). Comparison only; target is proposed.]

relationships.relationship: Women, girls, sexuality and the law
relationships.evidence_note: Feminist legal and sexual histories sit in both fields: Backhouse (1991), Lévesque (1989), Dubinsky (1993), Strange (1995), Sangster (2001), and Little's study of the moral scrutiny of single mothers (1994, abstract read). Shared people are rosters, not edges. PhD context: 136 of 155 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_women_gender (88%; lift 3.52), counted after removing shared anchors (Mitchinson). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relationships.relationship: Youth, normality and the psy-sciences
relationships.evidence_note: Adams studies discourses on youth, delinquency, indecent literature and sex education as producers of heterosexual norms (publisher description); Gleason studies psychology and the normal family. PhD context: 74 of 142 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_childhood_youth (52%; lift 5.66), counted after removing shared anchors (Adams, Gleason). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relationships.relationship: Moral reform, racial purity and law
relationships.evidence_note: Valverde's reformers linked sexual health to racial purity (publisher description); Backhouse's Colour-Coded traces racism through law (title-level). PhD context: 72 of 149 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_immigration_ethnicity (48%; lift 3.99), counted after removing shared anchors (Backhouse). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

relationships.relationship: Disease, eugenics and the body as objects of regulation
relationships.evidence_note: Adams reads Ontario's 1918 commission on venereal disease and feeble-mindedness as targeting bourgeois-defined immorality as much as infection (abstract). McLaren on eugenics and Mitchinson on women and their doctors are title-level. Comparison with the medical history entry, not a claim that medical history is regulatory history.

relationships.relationship: Ethnohistorical method in Canadian native–newcomer history
relationships.evidence_note: Trigger’s Wendat/Huron history joins archaeology, ethnography and contact records (existing atlas source), and his 1986 survey describes historians, anthropologists, archaeologists, geographers and economists combining in ethnohistorical research that was being integrated into national history. Bruce Trigger is already on the Ethnohistory roster; this edge records a contribution, not a founding claim.

relationships.relationship: Indigenous history and native–newcomer historiography
relationships.evidence_note: Overlapping subjects and people (Dickason, Miller, Lutz), different centres: Indigenous history centres Indigenous historical authority; this field centres relations, policy and encounter, often from colonial archives. The Indigenous entry’s existing strand native_newcomer_institutions (Miller) is the in-atlas meeting point. Comparison only: neither field is a subset of the other.

relationships.relationship: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
relationships.map_label: Indigenous critiques: autohistory, othering and colonizing practices
relationships.evidence_note: Sioui proposes autohistory: Indigenous self-interpretation and transmitted traditions in historical discourse (interview, 1991). Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (Saskatchewan History, Fall 1998; read in full) argues that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, keep even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework. LaRocque’s 1999 dissertation criticises the ‘neo cross-cultural approach’ of Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk and others as still othering (PDF pp. 249, 102, 109, 30 n.). Fixico (2009, US) says the premise of ‘Indian–white relations’ must be turned over for an Indian point of view. Fixico and S. Miller write about US historiography; they are cited as parallel critiques, not as statements about the Canadian books listed here. No identity classification is recorded.

relationships.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
relationships.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the proposed Settler colonialism entry. Greer argues the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others; commercial penetration, the fur-trade mode, is another. Most native–newcomer works predate the settler framework and do not adopt it. PhD context: among 2009–2026 PhDs engaging this roster (two or more people cited), the share also citing Wolfe’s or Veracini’s settler-colonial works rises from 1 of 66 (2009–14) to 14 of 88 (2015–19) and 26 of 65 (2020–26), while engagement with the roster holds steady (16.1% → 16.0% of all PhDs). Bibliographies record consultation, not adoption.

relationships.relationship: Innis’s fur trade as a resource reworked by later historians
relationships.evidence_note: Innis made the fur trade an introduction to Canadian economic history (1930). Ray’s later reconstruction of Indigenous traders reorients that subject; a later UTP reissue of Innis carries Ray’s credit (catalogue only). Contribution of a subject and evidence base, not influence on the field’s interpretations. PhD context: Innis is cited by 82 PhDs, The Fur Trade in Canada by 48.

relationships.relationship: Aboriginal people as a labouring class
relationships.evidence_note: Lutz’s “After the Fur Trade: The Aboriginal Labouring Class of British Columbia” (1992) brings Indigenous wage and exchange labour into working-class history. One specific intervention; Canadian labour historians are not assumed to have adopted it. Distinct from the settler packet’s Burrill (2019) edge, which proposes a settler-order framework for the same field.

relationships.relationship: Gender, marriage and missions in fur-trade and colonial society
relationships.evidence_note: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Rutherdale’s gender and race in the mission field (2002) belong to both fields; Van Kirk also anchors the proposed women and gender entry. Comparison, no direction asserted.

relationships.relationship: Colonized bodies and Aboriginal health
relationships.evidence_note: Kelm’s publisher description reads health and healing through postcolonial conceptions of the body and the power relations of colonization, as ethnohistory. A specific overlap with the Medical & health history entry; optional.

relationships.relationship: Labroussian economic and social history at Laval
relationships.evidence_note: Savard (1974) says Ouellet owed a debt to Labrousse and Chaunu; Robert Mandrou prefaced Ouellet’s 1966 book (review heading). Dechêne trained in France in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert before her Paris doctorate (1973), published as Habitants et marchands (1974) (Charron, Dictionnaire universel des créatrices; formal supervision not asserted). Linteau (1983) says social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence but that his generation was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians. Specific contributions to the Laval and New France strands, not an Annales origin for Quebec historiography.

relationships.relationship: The modernist generation adopts social history
relationships.map_label: New social history and the modernists
relationships.evidence_note: Linteau (1983) describes his cohort adopting social history and serial sources (censuses, civil registers), becoming more quantitative, and widening the subject from French Canadians to Quebec’s whole population. Self-description of one generation.

relationships.relationship: French-Canadian national history and its revision
relationships.evidence_note: Groulx’s national history and the Montreal school’s Conquest belong to the national-narratives umbrella; Rudin’s opening sets the historians’ ‘normal’ Quebec against both nationalist history and politicians’ distinct society. Comparison only: the field is not reducible to national narrative, and the modernists rejected that frame.

relationships.relationship: Quebec labour and working-class history
relationships.evidence_note: Rudin names Rouillard among the historians he criticizes; Rouillard writes the history of Quebec unionism, and Copp and Bradbury write Montreal’s working class (cdn_working_class sources). Overlap in people and subject; no direction asserted. PhD context: 79 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 34.6, lift 2.28).

relationships.relationship: Catholicism and the Quiet Revolution
relationships.evidence_note: Rouillard’s ‘turn not rupture’ and the Catholic Action revision (now a strand here) connect this field to religion and secularization. Gauvreau anchors the proposed religion entry, which also proposes the specific contribution crr_rel_04 into the catholic_action_origins strand. Broad comparison; title and abstract level.

relationships.relationship: Women’s history in French
relationships.map_label: Collectif Clio and Quebec women’s history
relationships.evidence_note: Quebec women’s history (Collectif Clio 1982; Lévesque 1989, 1997; Baillargeon 1991, 2012) is primary here (Q38), and its authors also appear in the proposed women and gender entry, which keeps a specific critique edge (cwg_rel_03). Bédard and Goyette place Clio and Micheline Dumont in Quebec historiography’s ‘modernist’ part.

relationships.relationship: The Quiet Revolution as a Sixties subject
relationships.evidence_note: Rouillard’s abstract makes the early 1960s the contested hinge of Quebec history. Coordination edge with the proposed cdn_sixties entry, which lists quebec_historiography as related; the Sixties drafter may supply stronger evidence (e.g. Mills 2010). [Merged with c60_rel_02 from cdn_sixties: Behiels locates the Quiet Revolution's origins in postwar liberalism and neo-nationalism; Gauvreau's review describes the revisionist challenge to "the conventional ideology of the Quiet Revolution"; Mills's review follows Warren's 1968; Igartua contributes "The Sixties in Quebec". PhD context: 18 of 136 PhDs engaging this draft are at francophone universities. Target is proposed.]

relationships.relationship: Indigenous historical authority and settler-colonial analysis
relationships.evidence_note: Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge settler colonial studies. Kauanui asks that it rethink indigeneity. Comparison only: Indigenous history is not a subset of the paradigm, and the paradigm did not originate there. PhD context: 74 of 86 core-citing 2009–2026 PhDs also engage the 'Indigenous peoples, fur trade & the West' co-citation field (86% vs 20% of all; lift 4.26). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relationships.relationship: Indigenous scholars question a settler-centred field
relationships.map_label: Indigenous critiques of settler colonial studies
relationships.evidence_note: Konishi: Indigenous scholars critique or challenge the field and offer extra-colonial histories. Kauanui: engagement with the structure thesis must rethink indigeneity and Indigenous Studies. A specific critique alongside the broad comparison; it records no identity classification.

relationships.relationship: Colonial and settler colonial phenomena distinguished
relationships.evidence_note: Veracini argues that colonial and settler colonial phenomena must be analytically disentangled and read in dialectical relation. Hoxie presents settler colonialism as the most promising aspect of a postcolonial critique. Alternative for review: a directed contribution post → settler_colonialism on Hoxie's account. PhD context: 32 of 86 core-citing 2009–2026 PhDs also engage the 'Empire, colonialism & postcolonial theory' co-citation field (37% vs 24% of all; lift 1.58). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relationships.relationship: Challenges settler national narratives of empty land and peaceful settlement
relationships.evidence_note: Veracini's history of the concept describes earlier writing that placed pioneering in 'empty' settings and disavowed Indigenous presence. Regan's contents page names 'Deconstructing Canada's Peacemaker Myth'. Targets settler national narratives, not every national history.

relationships.relationship: Decolonization-era usage and later theory
relationships.evidence_note: Veracini dates a usage, until the late 1970s, naming a diehard hyper-colonialism challenged by anti-colonial insurgencies. Mamdani revisits the first postcolonial generation's political economy (Rodney) to ask how settler and native became political identities. Comparison: no line of descent from liberation politics to the later field is asserted.

relationships.relationship: Harris: dispossession explained geographically
relationships.evidence_note: Harris explains British Columbia's reserve system as geographical dispossession resting on state power, capital and settlers, rather than primarily on discourse. He later reflects on the boundaries of settler colonialism (postscript title). It keeps the existing spatial–Indigenous comparison edge_777 separate. PhD context: 21 of 86 core-citing 2009–2026 PhDs also engage the 'Environment, development & the state' co-citation field (24% vs 10% of all; lift 2.45). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relationships.relationship: A settler order framework for Canadian working-class history
relationships.evidence_note: Burrill proposes integrating settler workers' ongoing theft of Indigenous land into the story of the Canadian working class. One specific intervention; labour historians are not assumed to have adopted it. PhD context: 5 of 86 core-citing 2009–2026 PhDs also engage the 'Labour & the working class' co-citation field (6% vs 9% of all; lift 0.66). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relationships.relationship: Settler and native as political identities in Africa
relationships.map_label: African settler colonies and political identity
relationships.evidence_note: Mamdani analyses settler and native as colonial political identities from African history. Elkins and Pedersen's comparative volume (contents unread) is a second witness. Comparison only.

relationships.relationship: Slavery and Black studies critiques of settler–native frameworks
relationships.evidence_note: Garba and Sorentino argue that Tuck and Yang collapse a settler–native–slave triad. Sexton argues that decolonial sovereignty claims can circumvent Black radicalism. These are Black studies theory rather than Black history as the atlas entry defines it; the source node is a review decision.

relationships.relationship: Land, labour and elementary structures of race
relationships.evidence_note: Wolfe's AHR forum essay and later book compare regimes of race through land and labour. Title level only: the weakest proposal, optional.

relationships.relationship: Thompsonian class and culture in Canadian labour history
relationships.map_label: Thompson and the new labour history
relationships.evidence_note: McNaught’s 1981 title frames the decade’s Canadian labour writing as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’, and Kealey’s 1981 essay strongly defends class analysis and the study of working-class culture. A contribution of resources to the class_culture_community strand; no claim that Canadian historians adopted one Marxist theory. PhD context: E. P. Thompson is cited by 106 PhDs 2009–2026 (candidates.csv), The Making of the English Working Class by 56.

relationships.relationship: A national field within labour history
relationships.map_label: Canadian working-class history and labour history
relationships.evidence_note: Labour/Le Travail, founded by the Canadian Committee on Labour History in 1976, is described by Freeman as one of the world’s leading labour history journals, and Kealey engages US labour history (Gutman and Montgomery, 1990). The atlas’s labourhistory entry has no Canadian participants; this comparison links them without making the Canadian field a branch of any one national tradition.

relationships.relationship: US new labour history and Canadian working-class history
relationships.map_label: Gutman, Montgomery and Canadian labour history
relationships.evidence_note: Kealey’s 1990 ILWCH essay on the politics and direction of Gutman’s and Montgomery’s US labour history (both on the atlas’s New Left roster) is a dated engagement. Title-level only; an influence direction is not asserted. Optional.

relationships.relationship: Feminist challenge to a ‘masculinist’ working-class history
relationships.evidence_note: Sangster (2000): feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history, and later calls to integrate race and ethnicity, shifted the field’s narrative and paradigms, integrating gender more effectively though not completely into class formation. A critique that also remade the field (Parr 1990; Bradbury 1993).
relationships.review_flag: women and gender history -> working-class history as both contribution (Parr) and critique (Sangster 2000): two claims on one directed pair; the reviewer should keep both or choose one
